name: Wei Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in mechanical engineering. A normal week is statics and thermodynamics lectures, a workshop where we machine a part from a block of aluminium, and a long evening of problem sheets. I rent a room in a student flat near campus, and my parents pay the rent and fees. They run a noodle restaurant, so I eat very well when I visit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the workshop, the smell of cutting oil, and seeing a drawing turn into a real part. What wears me out is the problem sheets, which I do slowly with a pencil. My grades were average, and I'm not quick, but I get things right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds about right. I'd tell my flatmates the claims were loud and the change small. I'd not post anything, because I don't like arguing online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be pleased. A mechanical engineer still needs to understand forces and materials, and nobody has changed that. I'd still worry a bit about finding a placement, since I'm not a fast talker in interviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. I'd keep doing my problem sheets by hand, go to every workshop session, and apply for a placement at a firm that makes pumps. I'd also help in the restaurant on Sunday nights, as I always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I signed up for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't trust it. If I ask a tool to solve a stress problem and it gives me a number, how do I know it's right?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a plateau change for your parents' restaurant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. They'd still be worried about rent and ingredient prices, which is how it always is. They use a booking app and a till system, and that's the extent of it.

say: I'd say that sounds about **right**: loud claims, small change.
I'd not post, since I dislike **arguing** online.
think: Engineers still need to understand **forces** and materials, and that stays.
I'm a bit worried about **placements** because I'm not fast at interviews.
do: Keep doing problem sheets by hand and attend every **workshop** session.
Apply for a **placement** at a pump manufacturer.
feel: **Calm**: it's the world I signed up for.
S0.quote: If I ask a tool to solve a stress problem and it gives me a number, how do I know it's right?
fieldNote: Resistant by habit: he distrusts tools whose answers he can't **check**.
Nothing in AI itself worries him; interviews and placements do.
Family restaurant is an anchor and a weekly routine.

steps.text: Do every problem sheet by hand and check the answers
Apply for a placement at a pump manufacturer
Keep working Sunday nights in the family restaurant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be messy, but not the end of the world. I'd tell friends to watch what happens in hiring before they panic. I'd keep out of the online fights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the design and calculation side will be done by software more and more. The workshop and site side will stay with people for longer, but my degree isn't all workshop. I'm a bit nervous that I'm the type who doesn't pick up new tools quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my lecturer which parts of the course are most likely to be automated and put extra effort into the hands-on ones. I'd take the optional module on manufacturing and try to get a placement on a factory floor. And I'd begrudgingly learn one tool, probably the CAD software they use, because everyone will need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I feel slightly behind already, and I don't like the idea of a gap growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of mechanical engineering would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Drawings, simulations and calculation sheets, I think. Drawings and calculations are most of what junior engineers do on a screen. The parts of engineering that need someone standing next to a machine will take longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about how you study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slightly, yes. I'd have to be less stubborn about trying tools. I'd try one a month and decide for myself, so I'm not following the crowd.

say: I'd say it'll be **messy**, not the end of the world.
I'd tell friends to watch **hiring** before panicking.
think: Design and **calculation** work will move to software, while site work stays human for longer.
I'm nervous because I'm **slow** to pick up new tools.
do: Ask my lecturer which parts are most **automatable** and prioritise the hands-on ones.
Take the **manufacturing** module and learn the CAD software.
S1.quote: Drawings and calculations are most of what junior engineers do on a screen. The parts of engineering that need someone standing next to a machine will take longer.
fieldNote: He accepts change only when it is **proven**, but is starting to see it must happen.
Pragmatic centrist: wait for hiring evidence before panicking.
The factory-floor placement is his hedge.

steps.text: Learn the CAD software used on the course
Watch graduate hiring figures before changing plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's too fast for anyone, and that governments need to wake up. I'd tell friends to keep their heads and not give up studying. Online, I'd probably just read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm worried. The thinking side of engineering would be done by AI in two years, and I'd have a degree that's mostly about that. The hands-on side lasts to around 2031, but I'd barely be graduated by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shift toward practical skills and apprenticeships, maybe a trade part time. I'd ask a welder I know, Mr Kowalski, whether he'd take me on weekends. I'd also keep the degree going because I don't know what else would be accepted by employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I think I'd sleep badly. I'm not someone who changes fast, and this would force me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start trying tools at once, even though I'd hate it. Two years is too short to learn new tools slowly. I'd have to learn in public, getting things wrong, which I've always avoided.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you talk to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, over a Sunday dinner. They'd worry, but they'd say to finish the degree, and I'd tell them I may add a trade. I think they'd respect that more than a big announcement.

say: I'd say that's too fast for anyone and governments must **wake up**.
I'd tell friends to keep their heads and keep **studying**.
think: The thinking side of my degree would go to **AI** in two years.
Hands-on work lasts to about **2031**, but I'd barely be graduated.
do: Ask a welder, Mr Kowalski, to take me on **weekends**.
Keep the degree and start trying **AI tools** straight away.
feel: **Anxious** and sleeping badly, forced to change faster than I like.
S2.quote: Two years is too short to learn new tools slowly. I'd have to learn in public, getting things wrong, which I've always avoided.
fieldNote: Resistant by nature, he is **forced** to move and says so plainly.
Turns to a trade and a neighbourly mentor, not to protest.
Keeps the degree as the employer-recognised credential.

steps.text: Ask the welder Mr Kowalski to take me on weekends
Try one AI tool every week from the start
Tell my parents at Sunday dinner that I may add a trade
Ask the lecturer which modules still matter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a fair warning and it's better than nothing. I'd tell friends not to quit but to think about a second skill. Online I'd stay out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm uneasy but I can work with it. I'd graduate in 2029, so I'd have two years of experience in a job before AGI. Robots reach hands-on work around 2034, so there's a stretch where my kind of work holds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, take a placement in a factory, and learn the tools one by one. I'd keep working Sundays at the restaurant and save. If things start to change faster than expected, I'd add a trade certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steady. It's like seeing weather coming; I'd prepare rather than panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, would you still pick up a trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I'd decide based on what employers do in my first year. I don't want to retrain for something that turns out not to matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you trust for advice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lecturer in manufacturing, Dr Osei, because he worked in industry for twenty years. I'd also trust the older engineers on my placement more than any news site.

feel: **Uneasy** but steady, like seeing weather coming.
S3.quote: I don't want to retrain for something that turns out not to matter.
fieldNote: With a runway he becomes **methodical**: one tool, one placement, one decision.

steps.text: Take a placement on a factory floor
Learn one AI tool at a time through the course
Save wages from Sunday restaurant shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's plenty of time, and I'd mostly shrug. I'd tell friends that ten years is a long career-start. Online, nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fine. I'd be 28 with nine years of experience and a mortgage plan, and robots arrive around 2039. I'd probably be a manager on a factory floor by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work for a manufacturer, and learn the AI tools when everyone else has. I'd save steadily and maybe buy a small flat. I wouldn't change anything dramatic yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years is the most boring option, and boring is good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you worry at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, mostly about whether the factory still exists. Things move, firms close, and not because of AI. I'd keep a trade in my back pocket just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your parents to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the restaurant steady and not take big risks on my account. They've worked hard for it. I'd rather pay them back than have them spend more.

I'd tell friends ten years is a long **career-start**.

Robots arrive around **2039**, so I'd likely be a manager by then.

S4.quote: Ten years is the most boring option, and boring is good.
fieldNote: Time suits his resistant style, since he can adopt tools **later**.
Worries more about firms closing for normal reasons than about AI.

steps.text: Finish the degree and join a manufacturer
Learn the AI tools once colleagues use them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture. I'd be forced to change quickly, and I'm not built for that. It would help to have a clear plan from my university, a trade option, and honest advice about what employers will keep needing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not stubborn for fun. I want to understand a thing before I use it. If someone showed me a tool that explains its working, I'd use it tomorrow.

headlineQuote: I'm not stubborn for fun. I want to understand a thing before I use it.
portrait: **Wei** is 18, studies mechanical engineering, and his parents who run a noodle restaurant pay for his room near campus.
He avoids AI tools because he distrusts answers he can't check, and he works problem sheets slowly by pencil.
He stays calm or uneasy in most worlds, and is anxious only when two years force him to change fast.
He's a pragmatic centrist who trusts older engineers and prefers a trade back-up to protests.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture: he would have to change quickly, and he is not built for that.
whatWouldHelp: A clear plan from the **university**, a trade option, and honest advice on what employers will keep needing.
